newsitem.title: JAPAN: Telecom titan NTT hits U.S. snag on int'l business.
newsitem.headline: Telecom titan NTT hits U.S. snag on int'l business.

text.p: Japanese telecoms titan Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) appears to have hit a snag in its plans to enter the overseas telephone market later this year due to trade friction with the United States.

In what would have been its first taste of the international phone business, NTT said in January it aimed to launch a special service later this year to provide Japanese multinational corporations with telecoms links between their offshoots in Europe, the United States and Asia.

On Wednesday, however, NTT said the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had informed its U.S. unit, NTT America Inc, that it will delay granting it a U.S. licence to provide international phone services.
Japanese international carrier Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd (KDD) said its application for a U.S. licence to provide international phone services had been similarly delayed.
KDD said the U.S. Trade Representative's office, the Commerce Department and the State Department had asked that it be excluded from a simplified and speedy application procedure.
"We are very concerned about the delay in one country," NTT president Junichiro Miyazu told a news conference.
The company has already acquired telecom licences in Britain, Germany and France.

Japanese media reports linked the delay in licence approval to Washington's irritation with Tokyo's insistence on keeping a 20 percent ceiling on foreign investment in NTT and KDD and to U.S. pressure to open up Japan's telecoms equipment market.

As part of a sweeping World Trade Organisation (WTO) pact to open global telecoms markets to greater competition, Japan last month agreed to remove its 33 percent ceiling on foreign investment in most carriers and radio-based services.
But Tokyo, arguing that Washington and other WTO members were also keeping some limits on foreign investment, resisted U.S. pressure to remove its 20 percent ceiling on foreign stakes in NTT and KDD.
Analysts said taking a stake of more than 20 percent in NTT would anyway be tough, given that the government still owns about two-thirds of the former state-owned monopoly.

Miyazu said NTT would mull what steps to take together with Japan's Posts and Telecommunications Ministry but added that he did not anticipate any immediate impact on NTT's international business plans.
NTT last December won regulatory approval to enter international business as part of a restructuring that will split it into a set of companies under a holding company.
Miyazu said a proposed merger of long-distance carrier Japan Telecom Co Ltd and overseas carrier International Telecom Japan (ITJ), would spark an industry realignment in Japan.
The two firms said on Wednesday they could merge around October if they worked out an agreement by the end of March.
Miyazu said NTT -- widely viewed as an attractive candidate to join one of the world's three international telecoms consortia -- had no plans now to join any global alliance.
But he added: "We will tie up with various companies depending on services and regions.
